Bacillus cereus emetic syndrome is the top diagnosis: it classically follows ingestion of reheated starchy foods (especially rice), has an incubation period of 0.5–6 hours, and presents with prominent nausea/vomiting and crampy abdominal pain — matching the timeline and symptom profile precisely. Staphylococcus aureus is highly plausible given its similar rapid onset (1–6 h), toxin-mediated vomiting and cramps, and association with improperly stored cooked foods (e.g., reheated dishes left at room temperature). B. cereus diarrheal syndrome is less likely as its onset is typically 8–16 hours, but overlap exists and co-toxin production or mixed exposure cannot be excluded. C. perfringens has an incubation of 6–24 hours and predominantly causes watery diarrhea and cramps without prominent vomiting — making it moderately plausible but less well-aligned with the 2-hour onset and vomiting. V. parahaemolyticus is unlikely: it requires seafood exposure, has an incubation of 4–96 hours (median 12–24 h), and rarely presents this acutely; no seafood history was reported."}
